items.title: C’River Governorship: PDP candidate accepts Otu debate challenge
items.description: The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Cross River, Arthur Archibong, has accepted Gov. Bassey Otu’s challenge to an open debate. Archibong said he was ready to debate Otu at any time and venue the governor chose, provided Otu attended personally. The candidate spoke with journalists in Calabar on Tuesday, responding to a challenge issued by the state Commissioner for Information, Ekpenyong Cobham. “I am willing to honour the challenge to a debate, on one condition: that Gov. Bassey Otu will be there in person. “The people deserve to hear directly from those seeking to lead them, not from proxies,” he said. Archibong said he would not engage Cobham in a war of words, describing the commissioner as his brother and stressing he was not on the ballot. “Pastor Cobham is my brother. But he is not on the ballot, so I will not join issues with him,” he said. Cobham had earlier challenged Archibong to publicly debate the Otu administration’s policies, programmes and performance ahead of the 2027 election. Archibong also defended Arthur Jarvis University (AJU), which he founded in Akpabuyo Local Government Area, against recent criticisms. He described the allegations against the institution as politically motivated, saying AJU was established to contribute to Cross River’s development. He urged critics to focus instead on environmental sanitation, blocked drainages and emergency response, particularly the condition of Watt Market. He said: “Instead of chasing imaginary bedbugs in Akpabuyo, they should come and see the real crisis in Watt Market. “Go there today and see the filth, the stench, the blocked drainages, and traders selling beside refuse.” Archibong also alleged that inadequate resources were undermining emergency response, particularly the state fire service. “Our firefighters have no diesel. Our fire trucks have no water. And when infernos like the one at SPAR Mall happened, we are left helpless,” he said. The PDP candidate expressed sympathy for traders, workers and families affected by the recent fire at SPAR Shopping Mall in Calabar. He promised that his administration, if elected, would strengthen emergency response and provide firefighters with water, diesel and essential equipment. Archibong also questioned the economic benefits of the administration’s foreign investment trips and Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs). “After so many MoUs, show me how many have translated to successful projects that are addressing the pitiful situation of this state. “Where are the factories? Where are the jobs? Where is the relief for the ordinary man?” he asked. The candidate criticised what he described as Otu’s absence during crises, citing recent landslides and the SPAR Mall fire. “When landslides claimed lives and destroyed properties, and when fire swept through our businesses like the recent SPAR Mall crisis, the presence of our governor is nowhere to be found,” he said. On scholarships, Archibong said educational support remained a personal commitment rather than an instrument for political advantage. “Scholarships are a personal act of service. I will not bring charity to the marketplace just to score cheap political points,” he said. He urged voters to make the 2027 election a contest based on ideas, records, competence and service rather than money, intimidation or violence. Archibong said: “Cross River deserves a governor who will not govern from a distance or by proxy. “Our people deserve leadership that shows up, listens and delivers. Let this contest be about ideas, about track records, and about who is ready to serve.” The post C’River Governorship: PDP candidate accepts Otu debate challenge appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: France : une tornade fait une quarantaine de blessés et endommage 300 habitations
items.description: Une tornade d’une rare intensité a fait une quarantaine de blessés, dont deux en urgence absolue, et endommagé quelque 300 habitations, lundi à Pomas, village de l’Aude, dans le sud-ouest de la France, rapportent mardi les médias locaux, citant les autorités. Au lendemain du phénomène météorologique, les opérations de reconnaissance et de sécurisation se poursuivaient dans cette commune d’environ 1.000 habitants située dans le massif des Corbières, où d’importants dégâts matériels ont été constatés. Selon la préfecture de l’Aude, citée notamment par l’AFP, 75 sapeurs-pompiers étaient mobilisés mardi pour poursuivre les opérations de vérification, tandis qu’un audit des bâtiments était engagé afin d’identifier d’éventuelles fragilités structurelles et les risques d’effondrement. Les habitations endommagées doivent également faire l’objet d’opérations de bâchage, alors que plusieurs routes demeuraient interdites à la circulation et qu’environ 1.400 foyers étaient encore privés d’électricité mardi matin. Les images diffusées par les médias français témoignent de la violence du phénomène : toitures arrachées, maisons fortement endommagées et débris projetés dans les champs et les rues du village. Les secours ont travaillé durant toute la nuit et des sinistrés ont été accueillis dans la salle polyvalente de Pomas, avec l’appui de la Croix-Rouge. D’autres ont été relogés chez des proches ou dans des communes voisines. La tornade avait frappé Pomas lundi en fin d’après-midi, alors que plusieurs départements du sud-ouest de la France avaient été placés en vigilance orange aux orages par Météo-France, qui avait alerté sur la possibilité de phénomènes localement violents. Selon Météo-France, la France connaît en moyenne quelques dizaines de tornades chaque année, avec des intensités variables. L’organisme souligne toutefois que l’influence du changement climatique sur la fréquence, l’intensité et la répartition géographique de ces phénomènes demeure à ce stade incertaine. The post France : une tornade fait une quarantaine de blessés et endommage 300 habitations appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: 'Not an enemy:' Slovakia calls on EU for 'friendly' China competition
items.description: Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Tuesday that the European Union (EU) should pursue "friendly" competition with China rather than treat the country as an enemy and put up barriers. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. Fico said Slovakia was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally, arguing that greater competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to do better and outperform others. "I have a different view about relations between the EU and China. I don't think we should fight China by putting up barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to do better." The two leaders' discussions also covered the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and enlargement. On the EU budget, Fico said Slovakia supported maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. "We're even saying that some extra funding should be found for countries in the eastern part of the EU, which, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said, adding that a strong agricultural policy is another key Slovak priority. On an EU enlargement, Fico reiterated Slovakia's support for countries seeking membership, adding that all applicants must meet the required criteria. "That means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And that also applies to Ukraine," he stressed. Fico said Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, arguing that they had been preparing for EU membership for much longer. (With input from Xinhua)

items.title: Trump Plans to Buy Midterm Ads About His Own Record
items.description: P resident Trump gathered his top political advisers in the Oval Office early this month to solve a problem of riches: how to spend his super PAC’s $400 million political war chest with fewer than 100 days to go before the midterm elections. Republican strategists are concerned about Trump’s low approval ratings and voter anxiety about the economy. One person familiar with the Oval Office strategy meeting put it this way: “When the issues that you typically campaign on don’t move voters—or voters are pissed off at you about those issues—the question becomes: What do you campaign on?” Some GOP strategists favor focusing entirely on specific races in an effort to convince voters of the merits of individual candidates and local issues. But Trump himself has rejected that approach. House and Senate Democrats, the president noted during the meeting, will make their fall campaigns a referendum on him. His advisers told him that the poor polling reflects the fact that the voting public still does not know about many of his accomplishments—the dozens of new stock-market highs, a decline in fentanyl deaths, the “sealed” southern border, the increase in domestic-manufacturing production. The solution Trump settled on, according to three people familiar with the meeting, was to lean into the Democratic strategy of focusing on himself. The president ordered a series of television advertisements about his own record that will serve as a backdrop to the hundreds of individual House and Senate contests. Trump wanted what one person described to us as “environmental lift” ads—commercials that would focus on nationalizing the midterms broadly around his victories—and he suggested that the ad makers mine his own on-camera statements as building blocks. “Go look at the clips,” the president told his team, according to this person. “I cite accomplishments all the time.” That decision has resulted in a Trump midterm-election ad blitz that is set to be rolled out soon from MAGA Inc., the main repository of Trump’s political fundraising, according to people familiar with the discussions, all of whom insisted on anonymity to describe internal conversations. Most of MAGA Inc.’s spending is still expected to go to targeted House and Senate races, for which the group has been establishing teams to review polling, voter modeling, and message testing. “We are going to unload the guns on both chambers real soon,” one of the people said. But another person told us that because Trump will inevitably be part of voters’ considerations, highlighting his achievements makes sense. “I think everybody does understand that the president and his agenda are on the ballot to some degree,” another person told us. A spokesperson for MAGA Inc. told us that the group does not comment on internal deliberations or plans. Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told us that Trump is committed to maintaining the Republican majorities in Congress. “President Trump is cleaning up Joe Biden’s mess,” she said in a statement. “There is a great story to tell because the United States of America has never been stronger than under his leadership.” Trump’s decision to focus a portion of his spending on himself echoes President Biden’s decision in the fall of 2023 to launch a series of ads trumpeting his own legislative record, as he sought to increase his approval rating in advance of his reelection bid. But Trump is not on the ballot this fall, which presents new risks. A new strategy of touting Trump’s achievements could well backfire by aiding Democratic efforts to make each race about national issues at a time when Trump’s approval rating is at record lows. Yet given the midterm headwinds, Republicans may have little choice but to present their most effective communicator to voters. T he political climate —an economic election in which voters don’t feel that their life has gotten better, despite some positive indicators—is in many ways similar to what Democrats faced in 2010 and 2022, when the electorate blamed their party for the economic pain of the 2008 financial crisis and the coronavirus pandemic, respectively. But in other ways, the situation Trump faces is different. Polls show that voters aren’t just anxious about inflation; they are frustrated with Trump’s war of choice with Iran and concerned about government corruption. Before Trump’s first midterm election as president, in 2018, the Pew Research Center found that 51 percent of the country believed that the economy was doing well, including 13 percent who described the economy as excellent. By July of this year, only 22 percent felt that the economy was doing well, and only 3 percent described it as excellent. Trump’s economic approval rating hovered at about 50 percent in 2018 public polls. Most polls this year show that his standing has fallen into the 30s. Republican political consultants have voiced concerns both publicly and privately in recent weeks about the triumphant tone of some of Trump’s economic messaging. Democrats see a familiar dilemma. “You’ve got to take voters from where they are to where you want to go, and the only way to do that is to not dismiss in any way what they know—and what I mean by that is, you can’t go in playing ‘It’s Christmas Time’ when that’s the last holiday they can afford,” Rahm Emanuel, who worked for the Obama and Biden administrations and is a potential contender in the 2028 presidential election, told us. “They’re going to put you on mute.” In 2010, Barack Obama wrestled with this problem by alighting on a “car in the ditch” metaphor to explain why, after the 2008 financial crisis, the promised recovery still felt slow in coming. Yet even that formulation proved ineffective, Obama’s senior strategist David Axelrod told us. “We sort of abandoned it because what we found was even that was offensive to people, because it felt like we were trying to blame others,” he said. “What we learned very quickly is, you cannot jawbone people into feeling what they do not feel in their own lives, and Biden defied that to his own detriment.” Trump has shown much more interest in hyperbole than in complicated metaphors, branding his second term in office as a new “Golden Age.” While stumping last Friday for Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina, Trump spoke glowingly about his second term. “You have record manufacturing and auto plants being built right now in the United States and in South Carolina,” he said. “We have the greatest economy in our history. Now, some people haven’t seen it yet, but they will.” Axelrod noted that Trump argued at the same rally that his own polling “should be at 100 percent on the economy.” “If you’re the average person out there, you’re seeing that and thinking What planet is he living on? ” Axelrod said. “You have to acknowledge that people are struggling and this is a work in progress.” David Winston, a Republican strategist who works with congressional leadership, told us that key to the midterms is whether voters, when they walk into a grocery store, feel that they can manage at least a little bit better than before Trump returned to office. “So Republicans need to be talking about what actions they took in terms of the economy to at least get things moving in the right direction, and what the outcome has been,” he said. “This is one where it can’t be a laundry list of 35 talking points. This has to be one or two key things.” [ Read: How Trump left America vulnerable to cyberattacks ] Trump’s advisers are hoping to drive home a discrete set of facts about his accomplishments over the past 19 months. The list is likely to include new tax breaks for certain workers and seniors, the stock market’s rise over the past two years, the military’s boat strikes purportedly targeting fentanyl, and his efforts to “seal” the U.S.-Mexico border, to name a few. Rather than distance himself from congressional elections—the preference of some Republican candidates in swing districts—Trump has argued that he can drive turnout in those races by making himself the center of the conversation. Next month, he will host the Republican Party for a two-day “midterm convention” rally in Dallas aimed at nationalizing the November races as a choice between extreme Democrats and Republican accomplishments. Trump has asked his supporters to treat November as though his name is on the ballot. “What I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” Trump said on Friday in South Carolina. “Just say that I’m on the ballot one more time.” I n other, important ways, Trump is better positioned than either Obama or Biden were at this point in their midterm races. He has a massive cash advantage, thanks to his aggressive fundraising over the first year of his term that collected tens of millions from crypto companies, AI entrepreneurs, and traditional Republican donors. He also enjoys a sharply gerrymandered political map in the House that has created a new cushion of Republican-leaning seats after mid-cycle redistricting. And the Senate majority will be decided by races in Republican-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska, Ohio, and Iowa. Trump’s advisers have not yet indicated to Republican consultants how much money the president will spend on the midterms, according to people familiar with the matter. But the merits of Trump inserting himself into the election may be less important to some Republicans than the fact that MAGA Inc. is starting to spend. Some in the party have worried for months that Trump might hoard his fundraising for the 2028 presidential-election cycle—or for something else entirely. MAGA Inc. has begun work on a number of campaigns about specific House and Senate races for the fall. Much of that advertising is expected to feature negative attacks on Democratic candidates, the traditional role of independent super PACs. MAGA Inc. has commissioned polling and research, along with modeling in the targeted House and Senate races. It has also shared information with other independent groups, including the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund, which are affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota and Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana. In the early spring, Trump’s aides hoped to launch a disciplined sales pitch to voters focused on Trump’s accomplishments, only to have that effort largely derailed by the open-ended Iran conflict. Trump’s approval ratings have eroded further since then. Now is the president’s last chance for a do-over, and his team is projecting confidence that it can get it right. “Anybody that is saying we are headed for a shellacking absolutely can’t just read the numbers,” one of the people familiar with the Oval Office meeting told us. With early voting starting in the first weeks of October, Republicans are once again betting that more Trump is their best way to block Democratic hopes of a wave election.

items.title: We gave them our mandate, not our purse – Inusah Fuseini demands accountability from MPs
items.description: Former Tamale Central MP Inusah Fuseini has warned that allegations of MPs pursuing personal interests over the public good could erode confidence in Ghana’s democratic institutions. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, the Lands Minister said the 276 Members of Parliament have been entrusted with significant powers by more than 30 million Ghanaians. “We have over 30 million people in this country; 276 have been privileged that, in between the four-year terms, they take decisions on our behalf because we have trusted them to do so,” he said. He said MPs are expected to represent citizens’ interests, oversee the Executive, and ensure that public resources are properly managed. “We have trusted them to do so. So when the public begins seeing that these 276 persons that we have given the mandate to represent us and transact business on our behalf in Parliament, hold our purse, hold the executive accountable, pass laws for us, are doing that for themselves, have commodified that mandate that we have given them, and are trading in that mandate,” he stated. According to Mr Fuseini, such conduct would go beyond individual MPs and raise broader concerns about Parliament’s credibility. “That not only undermines their legitimacy, it also undermines and erodes public confidence and public trust in that institution, and that is what we are confronted with.” His comments come amid a heated public dispute involving Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin and GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi. Mr Gyamfi recently described some critics of GoldBod, including Mr Afenyo-Markin, as extortionists. Mr Afenyo-Markin rejected the allegations as false and defamatory and said he would pursue legal remedies over the attacks. The dispute followed the Minority Leader’s scrutiny of reported losses linked to the Bank of Ghana’s Domestic Gold Purchase Programme and GoldBod. The political exchanges have since escalated into threats of legal action and counter-accusations. For Mr Fuseini, however, the wider issue should not be reduced to the personalities involved. He said MPs who were elected to protect the public purse must remain focused on the interests of the people. “If that person was sent to Parliament to ensure that the resources are used judiciously and prudently, and that person now thinks that all of us do not matter, in so far as his pocket is lined, then we are in trouble,” he said. “Then the basic reason why we elected them in the first place goes, because they do not stand for us any longer; they are standing for themselves.” Mr Fuseini therefore urged the public to treat the allegations surrounding MPs as a serious democratic concern. “You see, and that’s why we should treat what we are hearing not as Alexander Afenyo-Markin, but as a serious concern that goes to the root of our democracy,” he said. He said the issue also touches on the constitutional promise of equal opportunity and prosperity for Ghanaians. “That promise will seriously be undermined if people do not pursue the collective interests, but are pursuing personal interests to the, I mean, disadvantage of the entirety of Ghana.”

items.title: ILERA EKO: LASHMA tasks media to drive health insurance uptake
items.description: By Sola Ogundipe The Lagos State Health Management Agency (LASHMA) has tasked journalists with driving public awareness and uptake of the state’s mandatory health insurance scheme, warning that the policy cannot succeed if residents remain uninformed or distrust the system. The agency’s Permanent Secretary, Dr. Emmanuella Zamba, who gave the charge at a two-day capacity-building programme for journalists on the Lagos State Health Scheme and Ilera Eko, said the media must become a stronger force for explaining health insurance, challenging misinformation, exposing gaps and holding institutions accountable. “Policies alone do not guarantee success; their effectiveness depends on understanding, cooperation and participation, the media therefore has a critical responsibility to explain policies accurately, dispel myths, amplify impact and hold institutions accountable.” Her message came as the state pushes ahead with mandatory health insurance for all residents under an Executive Order signed by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu on July 16, 2024. “In a megacity like Lagos, health insurance is essential to protecting residents from catastrophic healthcare expenses, providing peace of mind, strengthening the health system and promoting sustainable healthcare financing,” she said. She urged journalists to use their platforms to explain what ILERA EKO offers, how residents can enrol and access services, while also questioning shortcomings that could undermine confidence in the scheme. Zamba said LASHMA was investing in media capacity because public awareness and trust would determine whether mandatory health insurance translated into actual coverage. The agency trained additional 36 journalists following the 56 trained in February 2026 under the first phase of the initiative. The journalists, their family members and dependants, received one year of free health insurance coverage from LASHMA. The state has also increased its Equity Fund for vulnerable residents from N1 billion to N3 billion, financed through one percent of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. items.title: Les médias néerlandais démentent l’intérêt du PSV pour Ounahi
items.description: Le dossier Azzedine Ounahi au PSV Eindhoven connaît un nouveau rebondissement. Alors que la presse espagnole faisait état d’une offre officielle du club néerlandais pour le milieu de terrain marocain de Girona, De Telegraaf affirme que cette piste n’est actuellement plus d’actualité. Selon le journaliste Jeroen Kapteijns, Ounahi figurait bien auparavant sur la liste du PSV, mais le recrutement de Kodai Sano et Sven Mijnans aurait permis au club de compléter son milieu de terrain. Le PSV ne prévoirait donc pas, à ce stade, de recruter un nouveau joueur à ce poste. Cette information contredit directement celle publiée par Mundo Deportivo, qui assurait mardi que le club d’Eindhoven avait formulé une offre pour l’international marocain et se trouvait même en pole position pour l’attirer. Le montant de cette éventuelle proposition n’avait pas été précisé, mais le PSV n’aurait pas souhaité payer la clause libératoire fixée à 25 millions d’euros. Toujours selon la presse espagnole, les dirigeants néerlandais auraient voulu accélérer les discussions avec Girona afin de devancer la concurrence. Une version désormais remise en cause par Kapteijns, qui assure qu’Ounahi n’est plus une priorité pour le PSV. Le Marocain reste néanmoins associé à plusieurs clubs durant ce mercato. L’Ajax s’est notamment intéressé à son profil, avec la possibilité de retrouver son ancien entraîneur Míchel. Hull City, Ipswich Town et Ittihad Club ont également été cités parmi les prétendants. De son côté, le PSV aurait désormais d’autres priorités pour renforcer son effectif, notamment aux postes d’avant-centre et d’ailier. Pour Ounahi, la piste néerlandaise semble donc, pour l’instant, s’éloigner. The post Les médias néerlandais démentent l’intérêt du PSV pour Ounahi appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: We should take these concerns from Afenyo-Markin and others seriously – Inusah Fuseini
items.description: Former Tamale Central MP, Inusah Fuseini, has called for serious attention to allegations of extortion involving MPs, saying the concerns go beyond individual politicians and could undermine public trust in Ghana’s democracy. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, the Lands Minister said allegations that elected representatives are using their positions for personal gain should not be dismissed as political attacks. He was commenting in the wake of allegations made by Sammy Gyamfi, the Acting CEO of the Ghana Gold Board, against Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin. Mr Afenyo-Markin strongly rejected the allegation and subsequently threatened legal action against Mr Gyamfi. The matter later escalated into a legal and political dispute, with Mr Afenyo-Markin filing a defamation suit against Mr Gyamfi. Against that backdrop, Mr Fuseini said the concerns raised about the conduct of lawmakers must be examined in the broader context of public trust in Parliament. He said Ghana has entrusted 276 Members of Parliament with significant responsibilities, including overseeing public resources and passing laws. “We have over 30 million people in this country; 276 have been privileged that, in between the four-year terms, they take decisions on our behalf because we have trusted them to do so,” he said. Mr Fuseini warned that public confidence would suffer if lawmakers were perceived as using their positions for personal gain. “So when the public begins seeing that these 276 persons that we have given the mandate to represent us and transact business on our behalf in Parliament, hold our purse, hold the executive accountable, pass laws for us, are doing that for themselves, have commodified that mandate that we have given them, and are trading in that mandate,” he said. “That not only undermines their legitimacy, it also undermines and erodes public confidence and public trust in that institution, and that is what we are confronted with.” The former Lands Minister said the central issue should therefore not be whether the allegations concern Mr Afenyo-Markin or any other individual lawmaker. “That, so if that person was sent to Parliament to ensure that the resources are used judiciously and prudently, and that person now thinks that all of us do not matter, in so far as his pocket is lined, then we are in trouble,” he said. He argued that such conduct would defeat the purpose for which Ghanaians elect their representatives. “Then the basic reason why we elected them in the first place goes, because they do not stand for us any longer; they are standing for themselves.” Mr Fuseini said the allegations should therefore be treated as a broader democratic concern. “And that’s why we should treat what we are hearing not as Alexander Afenyo-Markin, but as a serious concern that goes to the root of our democracy,” he said. He added that the issue touches on the constitutional promise of equal opportunity and national prosperity. “That promise will seriously be undermined if people do not pursue the collective interests, but are pursuing personal interests to the, I mean, disadvantage of the entirety of Ghana.”

items.title: Africa must harness technology to fix healthcare crisis — Adereni
items.description: … As CareCode Hackathon awards ₦10m to young African innovators By Sola Ogundipe Africa has been admonished to move beyond dependence on imported healthcare technologies and build solutions around its own health challenges. Making the call in Lagos during the MedVerge 2.0 health technology gathering hosted by three health initiatives: HelpMum, Dobic Health, and SmartMRS, Dr. Abiodun Adereni, the convener, said the continent had the talent, technology and enormous healthcare challenges required to develop solutions that could improve access, efficiency and quality of care. Addressing participants, Adereni, said the MedVerge initiative brings together the three healthcare ventures which he founded: HelpMum Africa, which uses technology and AI to tackle maternal and child health challenges; Dobic Health, which is expanding access to technology enabled clinical services; and SmartMRS, an AI powered electronic medical records platform designed to digitise healthcare operations and improve patient care. “MedVerge is a platform for convergence. We have the talent, we have the problems that need solving, what we need is stronger collaboration and the confidence to develop solutions around our own realities,” Adereni said. He argued that African countries should not wait for solutions developed elsewhere before addressing their healthcare challenges. “MedVerge was created to bring healthcare and technology professionals together, expose young African professionals to emerging technologies and demonstrate how locally developed solutions could address local health problems,” he said Noting that the convergence of the three platforms was deliberate, he identified sustainability as one of the biggest challenges facing health innovation in Africa. “We don’t collaborate enough; stronger collaboration is needed among governments, technology companies, healthcare providers, development organisations and innovators.” he said. He urged the health sector to learn from the tech and financial services sectors for integration of platforms and ecosystems, even as he called for successful innovations to be transferred to the government and integrated into public health programmes. “If an innovation has demonstrated value, the government should be able to adopt it, scale it and sustain it as a public health asset,” he said. Such an approach, he argued, would allow innovations developed by African organisations to reach larger populations instead of remaining small pilot projects. Speaking during a fireside session titled “The Days Ahead Are Tough,” moderated by Deborah Oguike, Adereni reflected on his decade of building businesses at the intersection of healthcare, technology and infrastructure. He said expanding health insurance coverage would provide the financial foundation needed to drive innovation and improve access to quality healthcare. He also disclosed his ambition to acquire a licensed Health Maintenance Organisation and use it to expand Dobic Health’s modern healthcare facilities across Africa. “Health insurance is the factor that will help scale healthcare innovations. I don’t see AI replacing doctors, but I see it making the work of clinicians faster and more efficient in diagnosis,” he said. Adereni said Nigeria should aim to become a producer and exporter of health technology rather than remain largely a consumer of solutions developed outside the continent. “Nigeria should not simply be a market for health technology developed elsewhere. We should be a place where health technology is developed, tested, improved and scaled,” he said. He argued that Nigeria needed policies that encourage technology adoption, sustainable financing, better infrastructure and stronger partnerships between government and innovators. The broader message from MedVerge was that Africa’s healthcare future cannot be built entirely by Importing solutions. It has to be built from within. CareCode Hackathon awards ₦10m to young innovators In a related development. HelpMum Africa has awarded ₦10 million to three young teams whose innovations emerged from its CareCode Hackathon, an initiative aimed at promoting technology driven solutions to healthcare challenges in Nigeria and across Africa. The hackathon brought together young innovators to develop and pitch products and ideas focused on the future of healthcare. Five teams – HerPride, Lavender Care, ChopBeta, Bumply and MamaConnect, made it to the final stage of the competition. At the end of the competition, Lavender Care emerged as the top beneficiary, receiving ₦5 million, ChopBeta won ₦3 million and Bumply received ₦2 million. The awards formed part of broader efforts by HelpMum Africa and its partners to encourage young people to apply technology and innovation to some of the continent’s most pressing healthcare challenges. The initiative was highlighted alongside a second panel session, “AI’s Next Chapter in Healthcare,” which brought together leading health technology founders to examine the growing role of artificial intelligence in healthcare and its potential to reshape how health services are delivered. HelpMum Africa, Dobic Health and SmartMRS reaffirmed their commitment to supporting healthcare innovation, entrepreneurship and technology driven solutions across Nigeria and the continent. The post Africa must harness technology to fix healthcare crisis — Adereni appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: China, US hold third Track 1.5 Dialogue in Beijing
items.description: China and the United States held the third Track 1.5 Dialogue in Beijing on Tuesday. The two sides engaged in candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges, and underscored that the China-US relationship is of vital importance and is currently at a critical juncture. Both sides expressed the need to jointly implement the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state, build on the new positioning of the China-US constructive relationship of strategic stability, strengthen communication and dialogue, and enhance mutual political trust. Representatives also called for promoting exchanges and cooperation in such areas as economy and trade, people-to-people and cultural ties, subnational cooperation, healthcare, artificial intelligence and food security, to properly handle differences and jointly address global challenges. The dialogue was co-hosted by the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and the Asia Society of the United States. Liu Haixing, head of the International Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the event and delivered a keynote speech. Approximately 40 Chinese and US representatives participated in the dialogue, including personnel from relevant Chinese government departments, local governments, think tanks and universities, as well as US strategic and business community figures like John L. Thornton, co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society.

Mr Fuseini warned that such conduct could undermine Parliament’s legitimacy and erode public trust in the institution. “That not only undermines their legitimacy, it also undermines and erodes public confidence and public trust in that institution, and that is what we are confronted with,” he said. He said MPs were elected to ensure public resources were managed in the interest of Ghanaians. “That, so if that person was sent to Parliament to ensure that the resources are used judiciously and prudently, and that person now thinks that all of us do not matter, in so far as his pocket is lined, then we are in trouble,” he said. Mr Fuseini said the central issue should therefore be the integrity of Parliament and whether elected representatives continue to serve the people’s interests. “Then the basic reason why we elected them in the first place goes, because they do not stand for us any longer; they are standing for themselves,” he said. He urged Ghanaians to view the allegations in that broader context rather than as a dispute involving Mr Afenyo-Markin alone. “You see, and that’s why we should treat what we are hearing not as Alexander Afenyo-Markin, but as a serious concern that goes to the root of our democracy,” he said. items.title: Lutte contre le trafic de stupéfiants: 5 000 plaquettes de tramadol saisies par la Police nationale
items.description: BURKINA-OUBRI-SAISIE-TRAMADOL Lutte contre le trafic de stupéfiants: 5 000 plaquettes de tramadol saisies par la Police nationale Ouagadougou, 25 août 2026 (AIB)- La Police nationale, à travers l’Antenne régionale de l’Unité anti-drogue (AR-UAD) de Oubri a saisi 5 000 plaquettes de tramadol, d’une valeur estimée à 8,5 millions de FCFA, et démantelé un réseau de trafiquants spécialisés dans la vente de produits prohibés. Selon les éléments recueillis par la Police nationale, les membres du réseau s’approvisionnaient en tramadol dans une commune frontalière de la province du Ganzourgou. Ils conditionnaient ensuite les comprimés dans des sachets noirs, qu’ils dissimulaient dans des effets d’habillement avant de les placer dans des sacs noirs. Pour échapper aux contrôles des forces de sécurité, les trafiquants privilégiaient les pistes rurales et roulaient à vive allure à bord de leur véhicule. Les produits étaient ensuite acheminés vers Ouagadougou, où ils étaient destinés à la revente, notamment à une clientèle composée en grande partie de jeunes. L’intervention des enquêteurs a permis de saisir un véhicule Toyota, deux sacs contenant les 5 000 plaquettes de tramadol, ainsi qu’une somme d’argent en numéraire. La valeur de la drogue saisie est estimée à 8,5 millions de FCFA. La Police nationale salue la collaboration des populations, dont les informations ont contribué au démantèlement de ce réseau. Elle invite les citoyens à maintenir leur vigilance et à poursuivre la dénonciation des comportements suspects. Pour signaler tout cas suspect, la Police rappelle que les numéros verts 17, 16 et 1010 restent disponibles. La Police nationale, une force publique au service des citoyens. Agence d'information du Burkina Source: Police Nationale

items.title: Nazinon/Examens scolaires et professionnels: le bilan jugé satisfaisant par le DREPPNF
items.description: BURKINA-NAZINON-BILAN-EXAMENS-SCOLAIRES-PROFESSIONNELS Nazinon/Examens scolaires et professionnels: le bilan jugé satisfaisant par le DREPPNF Nobéré, 21 août 2026 (AIB) – Le directeur régional de l’Education préscolaire, primaire et non formelle (DREPPNF) du Nazinon, Adama Congo, a jugé satisfaisant le bilan des examens scolaires et professionnels de l’année scolaire 2025-2026, vendredi à Nobéré, à l’occasion de l’atelier consacré à l’évaluation de leur organisation et de leurs résultats. L’atelier a réuni des participants venus des trois provinces de la région, à savoir le Bazèga, le Nahouri et le Zoundwéogo. Au cours des travaux, l’inspecteur Issa Sawadogo, chef du service des examens et concours, a présenté les données statistiques relatives aux différents examens. Au Certificat d’études primaires (CEP), la région du Nazinon a enregistré un taux de réussite de 97,09 %. Sur 18 032 candidats présentés, 17 507 ont été déclarés admis. « Nous sommes fiers du travail abattu par l’ensemble des acteurs. Avec un taux de 97,09 %, la région du Nazinon se classe deuxième au plan national. C’est la preuve que les efforts consentis portent leurs fruits », s’est réjoui le DREPPNF, Adama Congo. Le bilan des examens professionnels, notamment le Certificat d’aptitude pédagogique au professorat des écoles (CAPPE) et le Certificat supérieur d’aptitude pédagogique (CESAPé), a également été jugé satisfaisant. Les participants ont aussi échangé sur l’Évaluation certificative de l’éducation non formelle (ECENF). La présentation des statistiques a fait ressortir une hausse significative du nombre de candidats. Les candidats libres ayant pris part aux épreuves ont tous été déclarés admis. À cette occasion, Camarade Congo a invité les acteurs de l’éducation à promouvoir davantage l’utilisation des langues nationales dans leurs localités respectives. Abordant les conditions nécessaires à la réussite des activités pédagogiques, le directeur régional a également appelé les participants à œuvrer au renforcement de la cohésion sociale. « Soyez tolérants, soyez des communicateurs. La cohésion sociale est un gage de la réussite de nos activités pédagogiques. Cela vous aidera à traiter avec la plus grande diligence vos différends et vos difficultés », a-t-il recommandé. L’atelier a par ailleurs permis d’identifier des difficultés dans l’organisation des examens, notamment l’insuffisance de certains matériels dans les Circonscriptions d’éducation de base (CEB) et l’absence de budget consacré à la sécurisation du transport des sujets. Selon les participants, des directeurs provinciaux ont ainsi été contraints d’assurer le dépôt des enveloppes contenant les sujets dans certaines communes, sans accompagnement sécuritaire. Des propositions ont été formulées en vue d’améliorer l’organisation et la sécurisation des examens au titre de l’année scolaire 2026-2027. Agence d’information du Burkina IK/BGB/bak

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Culture: A Mané, l’histoire locale présentée comme un levier de résilience et de développement
items.description: SANDBONDTENGA-MANE – HISTOIRE-RÉSILIENCE- DÉVELOPPEMENT Sandbondtenga/Culture: A Mané, l’histoire locale présentée comme un levier de résilience et de développement Mané, 22 août 2026 (AIB) – L’histoire du kombéré (canton) de Mané constitue un précieux levier pour renforcer la résilience des populations, préserver la mémoire collective et stimuler le développement local, a estimé samedi le professeur d’histoire-géographie Harouna Sawadogo, lors d’une conférence publique organisée à l’occasion de la première édition du « Bayir Dare », à Silmidougou, chef-lieu dudit canton. Placée sous le thème « Le kombéré de Mané, un exemple de bravoure et de résilience face à l’impérialisme de Naaba Yasmé à Naaba Sinbdo », la conférence a permis au communicateur de revenir sur les grandes étapes de l’histoire du canton, de Naaba Yasmé, son fondateur, à Naaba Sinbdo, l’actuel chef. Le conférencier a relevé que les affrontements ayant marqué l’histoire ancienne du kombéré, bien avant la pénétration coloniale, s’inscrivaient principalement dans une logique de défense de l’intégrité territoriale. La résistance opposée en 1896 à la colonne Voulet-Chanoine constitue, selon lui, l’une des illustrations de cette tradition de bravoure. Cet héritage historique s’est prolongé à travers les différentes épreuves auxquelles les populations de Mané ont été confrontées au fil du temps, a-t-il soutenu. Abordant la période récente, Harouna Sawadogo a relevé la capacité des populations à faire face aux défis sécuritaires, notamment aux incursions terroristes enregistrées en 2022. Il a salué la résilience collective ayant permis la réinstallation de l’ensemble des villages de la commune à partir de 2024. Selon le professeur d’histoire-géographie, la connaissance du passé local doit davantage être exploitée pour favoriser le développement de la commune et promouvoir son potentiel touristique. Il a notamment appelé à une meilleure valorisation des ressources matérielles et immatérielles qui constituent le patrimoine culturel de Mané. Pour Harouna Sawadogo, la transmission de cette mémoire aux jeunes générations est capitale afin de leur permettre de mieux connaître leurs racines et de s’en inspirer pour relever les défis actuels. Cette conférence publique s’inscrit dans le cadre du « Bayir Dare », qui signifie « retour au village natal », une initiative visant à créer un cadre de transmission intergénérationnelle, à promouvoir les traditions locales et à renforcer les liens entre les ressortissants de Mané. La première édition a mobilisé les filles et fils de Mané, de l’intérieur comme de l’extérieur, autour de Sa Majesté le Naaba Sinbdo, chef du canton, dans une ambiance empreinte de fraternité et de solidarité. La cérémonie a également enregistré la présence des autorités administratives, militaires et paramilitaires locales, avec à leur tête Wendinconté Alain Kiemtoré, préfet, président de la délégation spéciale communale de Mané. Agence d’Information du Burkina WO/aio/bak

items.title: They’re standing for themselves, not us – Inusah Fuseini warns MPs over self-interest
items.description: Former Lands Minister and Tamale Central MP Inusah Fuseini has warned that allegations of MPs pursuing personal interests could undermine public trust in Parliament and Ghana’s democracy. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, Mr Fuseini said Parliament’s 276 members were given a clear mandate to represent the interests of more than 30 million Ghanaians. He said concerns that some lawmakers may be using their positions for personal gain should therefore be treated as a broader threat to democratic governance. “We have over 30 million people in this country; 276 have been privileged that, in between the times, four-year term, they take decisions on our behalf because we have trusted them to do so,” he said. Mr Fuseini said MPs are entrusted with significant responsibilities, including controlling public finances, holding the Executive accountable and passing laws. He warned that this mandate becomes compromised when lawmakers begin treating it as a personal commodity. “So when the public begins seeing that these 276 persons that we have given the mandate to represent us and transact business on our behalf in Parliament, hold our purse, I mean hold the executive accountable, pass laws for us, are doing that for themselves, have commodified that mandate that we have given them, and are trading in that mandate,” he said. According to him, such conduct would not only damage the credibility of individual MPs but could also erode confidence in Parliament as an institution. “That not only undermines their legitimacy, it also undermines and erodes public confidence and public trust in that institution, and that is what we are confronted with,” he said. His comments come amid a controversy involving Minority Leader Alexander Afenyo-Markin and Sammy Gyamfi. Mr Gyamfi, the Acting CEO of the Ghana Gold Board and NDC Communications Officer, had accused Mr Afenyo-Markin of extortion. The allegation triggered a fierce political dispute, with Mr Afenyo-Markin subsequently taking legal action. Mr Fuseini said the issue should not be reduced to a dispute involving one politician. He argued that the broader concern was whether elected representatives were still prioritising the collective interest of the people who sent them to Parliament. “If that person was sent to Parliament to ensure that the resources are used judiciously and prudently, and that person now thinks that all of us do not matter, in so far as his pocket is lined, then we are in trouble,” he said. “Then the basic reason why we elected them in the first place goes, because they do not stand for us any longer; they are standing for themselves.” Mr Fuseini said the allegations must therefore be viewed in light of the broader constitutional responsibilities of Parliament and elected officials. “That’s why we should treat what we are hearing not as Alexander Afenyo-Markin, but as a serious concern that goes to the root of our democracy,” he said. He said the pursuit of personal interests at the expense of the public could undermine the constitutional promise of equal opportunity and national prosperity. “That promise will seriously be undermined if people do not pursue the collective interests, but are pursuing personal interests to the, I mean, disadvantage of the entirety of Ghana,” he said.

items.title: Liptako: Le gouverneur salue la persévérance du promoteur du Marathon atypique de Dori
items.description: BURKINA-LIPTAKO-SPORT-MARATHON Liptako: Le gouverneur salue la persévérance du promoteur du Marathon atypique de Dori ‎ ‎Dori, 22 août 2026 (AIB) – Le gouverneur de la région du Liptako-Soum, Abdoul Karim Zongo, a salué, samedi à Dori, la persévérance et la résilience du promoteur de la première édition du Marathon atypique de Dori (MADO), Hama Hamidou Dicko qui a relevé avec succès le défi d’organiser cette compétition inédite. ‎ ‎Le Marathon atypique de Dori a réuni 45 coureurs issus des Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et de la population civile. ‎ ‎À travers cette compétition, les organisateurs ont voulu promouvoir les valeurs de paix, de résilience, de vivre-ensemble et de cohésion armée-nation. ‎ ‎La première édition du MADO s’est déroulée sur une distance d’environ dix kilomètres, parcourue sous forme de relais dans la ville de Dori par neuf équipes composées chacune de cinq coureurs. ‎ ‎Le camarade Hermann Venegda, membre de l’équipe « Entente », a été le premier à franchir la ligne d’arrivée. ‎ ‎Au classement général, l’équipe « Entente » s’est hissée sur la plus haute marche du podium, devant « Famille », classée deuxième, et « Paix », troisième. ‎ ‎L’équipe victorieuse a reçu des médailles d’or et la somme de 55 000 FCFA. La deuxième a bénéficié de médailles d’argent et de 45 000 FCFA, tandis que la troisième a été récompensée de médailles de bronze et de 30 000 FCFA. ‎ ‎Les quatrième et cinquième équipes ont également reçu chacune la somme de 25 000 FCFA. ‎ ‎Selon le promoteur du MADO, le camarade Dicko, l’idée d’organiser cet événement est née du constat de l’absence d’une telle compétition dans l’univers sportif de la région du Liptako. ‎ ‎Pour lui, la tenue effective de cette première édition constitue la concrétisation d’un rêve. ‎ ‎Il a traduit sa gratitude à l’ensemble des personnes et structures qui ont cru en son initiative et l’ont accompagné dans sa mise en œuvre, promettant de tirer les leçons de cette première expérience afin d’améliorer les prochaines éditions. ‎ ‎Le représentant des parrains, le camarade Namagnan Traoré, directeur régional de la Police nationale du Liptako, a salué une belle initiative ayant permis de rassembler les FDS et les populations civiles autour du sport. ‎ ‎Il a assuré de la disponibilité des parrains à accompagner l’événement afin de lui permettre de s’inscrire durablement dans le calendrier sportif régional. ‎ ‎Présidant la cérémonie, le gouverneur Abdoul Karim Zongo a salué la persévérance du promoteur ainsi que la résilience de l’ensemble du comité d’organisation. Le premier responsable de la région a également rendu hommage aux coureurs pour leur engagement. ‎ ‎Au regard de l’engouement et de l’enthousiasme suscités par cette première édition, le gouverneur s’est engagé à accompagner les prochaines éditions du Marathon atypique de Dori. Le MADO se positionne ainsi comme un nouveau cadre de promotion du sport et de consolidation de la paix, de la résilience et de la cohésion sociale dans la région du Liptako-Soum. ‎Agence d'information du Burkina ‎AMM/bak

items.title: Mayotte's Future Depends on Education, Not More Restrictions on Migrant Rights
items.description: Click to expand Image Children walk past modular classrooms built after Cyclone Chido, at the nursery and elementary school of Majicavo-Lamir village on the French overseas territory of Mayotte, on August 18, 2025. © 2025 Marine Gachet/AFP via Getty Images Students return to school this week in France’s overseas department of Mayotte. For most, the start of the academic year is a return to overcrowded schools that are often ill-equipped to meet their basic needs, and an education system that continues to fail thousands of children. A devastating cyclone in December 2024 worsened already persistent deficiencies in Mayotte’s education system. Efforts to rebuild classrooms have not successfully addressed these challenges, and many schools continue to operate on rotation systems. Even before the cyclone, thousands of children were excluded from education, a consequence of burdensome enrolment procedures and other barriers. At the start of the 2025 school year, the Mayotte Observatory on School Exclusion found that more than 15,000 school-age children were not in school, continuing a worrying upward trend. Others attend schools in conditions that fall short of basic standards, including access to water, sanitation, nutritious food, and a safe learning environment. Rather than addressing these persistent failures, political leaders have blamed Mayotte’s structural challenges on migration. Immediately after the cyclone, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to restrict undocumented migration, mainly from Comoros and East Africa. Just before students returned to school this week, Edouard Philippe, a former French Prime Minister and a 2027 presidential candidate, declared that he would suspend access to asylum droit du sol, the principle of citizenship by birth on French territory, and immigration based on family ties in Mayotte. These proposals are presented as solutions to the many challenges facing France's poorest department. Yet many of Mayotte's difficulties stem from longstanding structural inequalities, chronic underinvestment in public services, and exceptional laws that apply only on the island, including restrictive citizenship and immigration measures. Such policies have done little to improve living conditions or address the lack of access to housing, water, electricity, healthcare, and education faced by many residents, including children. They also raise serious legal concerns, as they conflict with protections guaranteed under French constitutional law, European Union law, and international human rights standards. As Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu begins two days in Mayotte, French authorities should move beyond migration-focused rhetoric and announce concrete measures to guarantee economic and social rights for all residents. Ensuring every child can go to school would be a far more meaningful investment in Mayotte's future than further restricting fundamental rights.

items.title: African health ministers meet to tackle challenges
items.description: By Damilola Samuel Health ministers from 47 African countries have begun discussions in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on measures to strengthen healthcare systems and improve the continent’s response to emerging health challenges. The three-day meeting, which opened on Tuesday, is the 76th session of the World Health Organisation Regional Committee for Africa and brings together health ministers, government officials, development partners and health experts. The meeting is expected to produce decisions that will influence health policies and investments across the region in the coming year. One of the major issues before the ministers is how African countries can secure more sustainable funding for healthcare at a time when many countries are dealing with limited resources and growing health needs. The ministers will also consider the Africa Health Workforce Agenda 2026–2035, which is aimed at helping countries train, employ and retain more health workers. Opening the session, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie called for African countries to rely more on their own capacity and strengthen cooperation rather than continue depending heavily on external support. “Africa’s next health chapter must be defined by ownership over dependency, integration over fragmentation and practical action over words,” he said. Ethiopia’s Minister of Health, Dr Mekdes Daba, said the continent must prepare its health systems for challenges ranging from climate change and emerging technologies to demographic changes, health inequalities and complex emergencies. The issue of health security is also high on the agenda as African countries continue to face outbreaks and other public health emergencies. The ministers are expected to consider a framework for strengthening national emergency medical teams so that countries can respond more quickly when outbreaks, disasters and other emergencies occur. The discussions come as the Democratic Republic of Congo battles its largest Ebola outbreak, highlighting the need for countries to maintain the capacity to detect and respond to infectious disease threats. The ministers will also examine proposals aimed at protecting Africa’s progress in the fight against polio by maintaining surveillance systems, laboratories, trained personnel and emergency response structures developed during the eradication campaign. WHO Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, said the decisions taken at the meeting would have an impact beyond the three-day gathering. “The decisions we take this week will shape policies, guide investments and influence future generations,” Janabi said. Another proposal before the committee is the creation of a Regional Health Data Hub, which is expected to help countries identify health threats earlier, improve the allocation of resources and use reliable data in making health decisions. The meeting will also consider a long-term framework, A New Era of Health for Africa: United Action for Vision 2035, which focuses on stronger primary healthcare, resilient health systems, sustainable financing, digital transformation and greater ownership of health programmes by African countries. The WHO said the outcomes of the meeting would guide its support to member states and strengthen cooperation among African countries as they work towards building more resilient and self-reliant health systems. The post African health ministers meet to tackle challenges appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Oranges, sardines and eggs could help protect people exposed to air pollution, Ghana study finds
items.description: For people who spend long hours beside busy roads, breathing polluted air is often part of the job. Street vendors, traffic officers, market traders, construction workers and other outdoor workers can spend hours each day exposed to exhaust fumes and other pollutants. Now, a new Ghanaian study suggests that what they eat could help their bodies cope with some of the damage caused by polluted air. The Dietary Intervention to Mitigate Air Pollution health effects among street hawkers and vendors in Accra (DIMAP) study, conducted by researchers from the University of Cape Coast, followed 307 street vendors in Accra for 12 months. The study was led by Professor Kofi Amegah, an Associate Professor of Environmental and Nutritional Epidemiology at the University of Cape Coast. One group of vendors received a weekly supply of foods including oranges, peanuts, sunflower oil, eggs and sardines, while another group continued with their usual diets. The vendors worked along some of Accra’s busiest roads, including Atomic Junction, Madina, Lapaz, Tetteh Quarshie, Kaneshie, Graphic Road, Makola and Kwame Nkrumah Circle. These are areas where thousands of vehicles pass every day, exposing people who work there to pollution for long periods. Prof. Amegah says this prolonged exposure is what prompted the research. “And then they are exposed to a high level of a dangerous cocktail of pollutants for very long hours. So it’s important that we protect their health. And that is the main reason why we conducted this experimental study to look at the effectiveness of nutrition intervention for mitigating or attenuating the health effects among the street vendors.” Air quality monitors used during the study recorded average PM2.5 levels of about 40 micrograms per cubic metre along the study routes. PM2.5 is made up of extremely small particles in the air. They are so tiny that they can travel deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream. Long-term exposure can increase the risk of heart and lung diseases, stroke and other serious health problems. The World Health Organization recommends that the 24-hour average level of PM2.5 should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. After following the vendors for a year, researchers found that those who regularly ate the antioxidant-rich foods reported fewer symptoms associated with air pollution. They were 55 percent less likely to develop a persistent cough, 60 percent less likely to experience difficulty breathing, and 81 percent less likely to suffer dizziness. The biggest difference was recorded in irregular heartbeat. Vendors who received the food intervention were 92 percent less likely to experience the condition. They were also 66 percent less likely to be admitted to hospital for the symptoms studied. Prof. Amegah, however, says the evidence should be viewed carefully. “The evidence is…supported by the biology. And the biology is that antioxidants are able to mop up free radicals, which are the pollutants.” Antioxidants are substances found naturally in many foods. They help the body deal with harmful substances that can be produced when pollution enters the body. The researchers therefore recommend increasing the intake of foods such as oranges and other fruits, vegetables, nuts, eggs, peanuts and foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, including fatty fish and avocado. Prof. Amegah says, “So we are advocating, or we are advising them to increase intake of antioxidant-rich foods like oranges, like all the fruits, vegetables, nuts, cooking oils, eggs, peanuts, etc., which are very rich in antioxidants like vitamin C, like vitamin E and selenium.” He also cautions that changing diets cannot replace efforts to clean up Ghana’s air. “So what we need to understand is that this is not a substitute for air quality regulations. So we need to have air quality regulations that will help to curb the air pollution problem in our area.” The findings come as Ghana continues to deal with air pollution from several sources, including vehicle emissions, open burning, household fuels and industrial activities. For people who work outdoors, avoiding exposure can be difficult because their income depends on being on the streets. Prof. Amegah says the solution must therefore combine personal protection with stronger action from government and local authorities. “So every street vendor across Ghana needs to protect themselves by, one, mitigating or minimizing their exposure by wearing nose masks, etc. And then also eating well, eating a balanced diet, and importantly, eating antioxidant-rich food.” But he says the greater responsibility lies in reducing pollution at its source. “Oh, the call on government is what we are saying, that they need to invest in air pollution control. They need to support the municipal, metropolitan and district assemblies. So that at least we can be able to address the air pollution problem, which is worsening in our space on a daily basis.” The researchers stress that the study does not mean people should simply eat oranges or sardines and continue breathing polluted air. Instead, they say better nutrition could be one part of a wider response while Ghana works to reduce the pollution that people are exposed to every day. For the thousands of people whose workplaces are Accra’s busy roads and markets, that wider response cannot come soon enough. This story was a collaboration with New Narratives. Funding was provided by the Clean Air Fund, which had no say in the story’s content.
